endorsements.quote: Involving regional educators in reviewing language, cues, and contextual details helps ensure authenticity and reduces the risk of cultural mismatch.

Validation should begin with expert review, in which subject matter experts examine AI outputs for clinical accuracy, alignment with current guidelines, and relevance to the local clinical and educational context ( 21 ).

Training should also address validation and quality assurance practices, enabling educators to systematically review AI generated content for factual accuracy, bias, and alignment with intended constructs.
Educators need a clear understanding of what AI systems can and cannot reliably do in assessment contexts, including commonly reported limitations and failure modes documented in the literature.
Workshops and short training modules can build these skills effectively ( Table 4 ).
Early adopters can support institutional rollout by mentoring colleagues and participating in communities of practice that encourage shared learning and reduce duplication of effort ( 15 ).
Institutions should use secure, institutional, or encrypted AI platforms and avoid public tools for generating or storing final examination content.

Faculty should ensure diversity across patient demographics, including age, gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, avoid stereotypical portrayals such as linking specific conditions or behaviors to particular groups, and include clinical conditions that reflect local epidemiology.
Performance data should be analyzed across variables such as gender, language, or educational background to detect differential item functioning.

After each assessment cycle, key psychometric metrics should be collected, including item difficulty based on score distributions, discrimination indices that indicate how well the station differentiates between higher and lower performing candidates, and inter rater reliability across examiners ( 24 ).
To facilitate this, institutions can develop case templates that standardize structure across specialties ( 21 ).

AI-generated cases should be housed within secure assessment management systems that maintain access logs, and case variants should be rotated across exam cycles to reduce predictability and content leakage.

unlisted_practices: Require subject matter expert review, blueprint cross-check, independent peer review, and pilot testing of AI-generated OSCE cases before use in formative or summative assessment.
Define assessment design parameters (station format, competency focus, timing, scoring structure) before prompting AI to generate OSCE cases.
Enrich AI prompts with clinical guidelines, local epidemiology, cultural context, and competency frameworks to improve content validity.
Document prompts systematically and refine them iteratively so AI-generated cases can be regenerated and reviewed in a controlled manner.
Generate supporting OSCE materials with AI only from a fully validated core case, and review all supporting materials collectively for internal consistency.
Generate validated case variants and rotate them across exam cycles to reduce content leakage and predictability.
Revise or retire stations showing evidence of unfairness or bias.
Maintain an audit trail of revisions, psychometric results, and rationale for changes to AI-generated cases.
Collect structured feedback from candidates, examiners, and standardized patients to iteratively revise AI-generated stations.
Adapt standardized patient scripts to locally appropriate communication styles and sociocultural norms.
Embed AI training into faculty development programs and share psychometric findings and lessons in training workshops.
Adopt a bias audit checklist for AI-generated assessment content.
Use AI as a complement rather than a replacement to faculty expertise in assessment design.

screen.reason: This is a guidance/tips article providing practical recommendations and a framework for medical educators on utilizing AI/LLMs to generate OSCE stations.
